title: Why the DeLisa drew crowds while the Grand Terrace declined
summary: Cheap setups and a rollicking atmosphere made the DeLisa popular as the Grand Terrace's higher prices lost custom.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Cabarets, honky-tonks and the Storyville nightlife scene

blocks.x: This was about the time that -- the place where Earl Hines played.
Grand Terrace, when that sort of went down.

It was getting ready to go into a demise then. See, I don't know, the Grand Terrace thing, it was -- see, people then didn't -- we weren't in any prosperous area -- I mean, era, at that time. We weren't in a prosperous era, and their prices, I think, were a little high and -- because, at the Del'esa, this is what attracted so many people to it. You could come in there and get a setup, a setup would be ice and your Cokes and a couple of root beers or something like -- I mean, not root beer, ginger ale. And you'd get that a bring a half a pint of whisky and two people could get in there for two dollars.

And then more people, and it would add up. But it wasn't no strain on the pocketbook. And then it had a different atmosphere to it. They had little knockers, and they'd beat on the tables because they didn't have the tablecloths, just a plain -- tables, and they would beat on the tables and it was just a rollicking time.
